idiom_name: generated proxy type plus one interception handler and a class cache
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: at a point where the subject's interfaces are known, ask the runtime to produce a type that implements them and routes every invocation into one handler that receives (proxy, method, arguments); the handler decides whether to forward to the target, add behaviour around the call, or answer without calling at all. Cache the generated type per interface set (creation is expensive and must not happen per call) and keep per-instance state in the handler, never in a shared handler. The handler must define behaviour for everything the type can receive, including identity methods, default methods and void or primitive returns, and it must decide explicitly how self-invocation and identity are handled.
code_sketch:
proxy_class = runtime.define_proxy(subject_interfaces)      # cached per interface set
proxy = proxy_class(handler(target))                        # per instance

class Handler:
    def invoke(self, proxy, method, args):                  # single interception point
        decide_and_forward(method, args, self.target)
        return result
pitfalls: Generating a proxy type per call instead of per interface set; the cache is the difference between a working design and an unusable one.
Routing only the 'interesting' methods: identity methods, default methods and void returns still arrive at the handler and must not be silently mis-encoded.
Sharing one handler, and with it one target reference, across every proxy instance.

Failing to handle Object methods (equals, hashCode, toString, clone, finalise): these arrive at the handler and must be handled deliberately; default forwarding often surprises callers who expect identity semantics from the proxy.

Creating a new proxy type for every instance instead of caching it per (interface set, classloader): proxy class generation is expensive (I/O, bytecode engineering, classloading) and must be amortised across all instances sharing the same contract.

Stacking a second proxy on a target that is already proxied by the same framework: the outer proxy intercepts the inner proxy's dispatch, adding latency and making stack traces harder to read without improving behaviour.

Baking the target reference permanently into a serialisable handler without accounting for the target's serialisation lifecycle: the handler may hold a reference to a session-scoped object that outlives its context.

Neglecting to override equals/hashCode on IProxyGenerationHook or IInterceptorSelector implementations (Castle DynamicProxy): the default Object identity breaks proxy-type caching and can cause unbounded proxy-class growth.

Wrong move: constructing a new ProxyGenerator (or asking the runtime for a fresh proxy class) at every call site -> each generator carries its own type cache, so identical contracts regenerate bytecode and CPU/memory climb in long-running processes -> reuse a single generator instance per process, as Castle DynamicProxy's own documentation warns.

Wrong move: expecting @Transactional-style advice to fire on a method the target calls on itself -> the self-call never enters the proxy, so the advice is silently skipped and the transaction or metric simply does not happen -> route the internal call through the injected proxy or an explicit self-reference.

Wrong move: casting an injected dependency to its concrete class because it works locally -> the container flips to a JDK interface proxy for that bean and the cast throws ClassCastException in production -> code against the interface, or pin the proxy mode explicitly in configuration.
